source: Bjork, R. A. (1994) Memory and metamemory considerations in the training of human beings (chapter in Metcalfe & Shimamura, Metacognition)
finding: Founding statement of desirable difficulties. Bjork lists manipulations that slow or worsen performance during training but improve long-term retention and transfer: varying conditions of practice, contextual interference (interleaving), distributing practice, reducing feedback frequency, and using tests as learning events. He says the learner is pushed into more elaborate encoding and more varied retrieval, i.e. more transfer-appropriate processing. He also argues that trainers are shaped like operant conditioning by trainee performance and satisfaction, so they drift to easy conditions.
numbers: Cites Bahrick (1979): 50 Spanish words, sessions 0, 1 or 30 days apart; the 30-day gap was worst on in-session tests but best on a test 30 days after training. Cites Hogan & Kintsch (1971): study trials won at end of session, test trials won after 48 h. Cites Landauer & Bjork (1978) on expanding retrieval. Cites Mannes & Kintsch (1987): an inconsistent outline hurt verbatim recall but helped inference questions. No new effect sizes; it is a synthesis.
quote: A variety of manipulations that impede performance during training facilitate performance on the long term.
limits: Review; the term is not yet a formal theory (no equations). Which difficulties are 'desirable' is defined by outcome (they help later), which makes the claim partly circular. Evidence is mostly verbal memory and motor skill.
agent_relevance: Core rule for our agent: a lesson, prompt change or schema step must not be judged by its immediate score. Also a warning that the trainer (here: our own tuning loop) is rewarded by easy early wins and drifts toward them.

source: Shea, J. B., & Morgan, R. L. (1979) Contextual interference effects on the acquisition, retention, and transfer of a motor skill. JEP: Human Learning and Memory 5(2), 179-187
finding: Original contextual-interference experiment. Subjects learned three arm-movement tasks (grasp a tennis ball, knock down barriers in a set order) in a blocked or a random schedule. Blocked was much better during practice. Random was better on delayed retention and on transfer, especially to the more complex transfer task. Blocked-trained subjects tested in a random order did worst.
numbers: 72 subjects (df = 68 for group effects). 54 acquisition trials in 3 sets of 18. Retention at 10 min or 10 days, 18 trials each. Acquisition errors: blocked M = 4.42 vs random M = 9.13 (F(1,68) = 23.75). Retention errors: random M = 2.10 vs blocked M = 4.33 (F(1,68) = 12.85), concentrated in the random retention sequence. The total-time gap between groups had nearly vanished by the last acquisition block. At 10 days blocked-blocked was slightly faster than random-random, so the benefit depends on the test format.
limits: Single lab, small groups, one motor task family. Test format matters: blocked learners did fine if tested blocked. Later motor-learning meta-analyses report smaller or inconsistent contextual-interference effects in some lab tasks (not opened here).
agent_relevance: Gives the template: an interleaved schedule hurts the practice-phase score by design. If our agent trains on mixed task orders, expect worse early curves and judge on held-out later tests in a changed format.

source: Simon, D. A., & Bjork, R. A. (2001) Metacognition in motor learning. JEP: Learning, Memory, and Cognition 27(4), 907-912
finding: The keystroke study. Participants learned three 5-key sequences on a number pad, each with its own goal movement time (900, 1200, 1500 ms), under blocked or random practice, and repeatedly predicted their own error on a test 24 h later. Blocked practice gave better practice scores and worse retention. Blocked learners predicted they would do better and were strongly overconfident. Random learners predicted accurately.
numbers: 48 UCLA undergraduates, 24 per group. Each reached 30 correct trials per pattern. Practice percent absolute constant error: blocked 5.68% vs random 8.85% (F(1,46) = 10.41); advantage shrank across 6 blocks and was significant only in the first 3. 24-h test error: blocked 19.68% vs random 10.80% (F(1,46) = 22.29, p < .001). Predicted error: blocked 8.19% vs random 11.87% (F(1,46) = 4.59, p < .05), i.e. blocked learners expected to do better. Predicted vs actual: blocked 8.19% vs 19.68%; random 11.87% vs 10.80%.
quote: blocked practice enhanced acquisition but harmed retention. Participants, though, predicted better performance given blocked practice.
limits: One motor task, 24 h delay only, college students. Questionnaire ratings of the schedules showed no interesting results (authors' footnote). Authors conclude people read current ease of access as a valid index of learning.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that a learner (or a model) judging its own progress during practice will be wrong in the blocked direction. For our agent: confidence during a lesson is not a safe signal; require a delayed, held-out check.

source: Kornell, N., & Bjork, R. A. (2008) Learning concepts and categories: Is spacing the 'enemy of induction'? Psychological Science 19(6), 585-592
finding: Learners studied paintings by 12 artists, either all of one artist's paintings together (massed) or mixed across artists (spaced/interleaved), then identified the artist of NEW paintings. The authors expected massing to help induction; interleaving won in every experiment. Participants mostly believed massing had been better, even after the test.
numbers: Exp 1a: 120 UCLA students, 6 paintings per artist, block order MSSMMSSMMSSM; spacing effect F(1,119) = 77.35, partial eta-sq = .39; first test block 61% spaced vs 35% massed, d = 0.99. Exp 1b: 72 students between subjects, F(1,70) = 15.63; first block 59% vs 36%, d = 1.28. 78% of participants did better with spacing, yet 78% said massing was as good or better. Exp 2 (80 students, 'familiar or unfamiliar artist' recognition, no names needed): spaced hit rate .77 vs massed .67, t(79) = 3.28, d = 0.41. With only 2 paintings per artist: same pattern. In Exp 2, 64 of 72 participants who saw a difference thought massing was more effective. Of 28 participants asked afterwards, accuracy on which artists were spaced was .74 (above chance) but .55 for massed (not above chance).
quote: In marked contrast to our expectations, spaced study resulted in significantly better test performance than did massed study
limits: Counter-case built by the authors: finding one shared word from 6 clue words (12 sets, 20 students) favoured massing, .34 massed vs .22 spaced, d = 0.65, because spacing made the problem nearly unsolvable. The authors link the effect to discrimination between categories; the benefit may not hold when the task is to detect commonality without needing to discriminate. Exp 2 effect is smaller than Exp 1.
agent_relevance: The flagship induction result: interleaving helps generalisation, not just rote recall, yet feels worse. Our agent should interleave problem types when learning categories, and should not abandon it because early accuracy is lower.

source: Roediger, H. L., & Karpicke, J. D. (2006) Test-enhanced learning: Taking memory tests improves long-term retention. Psychological Science 17(3), 249-255
finding: Students read prose passages, then restudied or took free-recall tests, with final recall at 5 min, 2 days or 1 week. Restudy won at 5 minutes; testing won at 2 days and 1 week. Students who restudied predicted they would remember more.
numbers: Exp 1 (120 students, 40 per cell): 5 min restudy 81% vs test 75% (d = 0.52); 2 days test 68% vs restudy 54% (d = 0.95); 1 week test 56% vs restudy 42% (d = 0.83). Interaction F(2,117) = 32.10, partial eta-sq = .35. Exp 2 (180 students): 1-week recall STTT 61%, SSST 56%, SSSS 40%; the SSSS group read the passage 14.2 times vs 3.4 for STTT. 5-min recall reversed: SSSS 83%, SSST 78%, STTT 71%. Proportional forgetting over a week: SSSS 56%, SSST 28%, STTT 14%. The SSSS group was more confident of 1-week memory than STTT (d = 0.61).
quote: restudying produced better recall than testing (81% vs. 75%)
limits: Prose passages and free recall, college students. First-test performance in the test conditions was below 100%, so results are not only extra exposure. The crossover (restudy better at 5 min) is the classic 'performance misleads' signature.
agent_relevance: The cleanest crossover: the strategy that wins at 5 minutes loses at 1 week. For our agent, any benchmark taken right after a prompt or lesson change can reverse sign at a delay.

source: Karpicke, J. D., & Roediger, H. L. (2008) The critical importance of retrieval for learning. Science 319, 966-968
finding: Students learned 40 Swahili-English pairs. Four conditions varied whether a pair was dropped from further study (N) or from further testing (T) after being recalled once. Learning-phase performance and predicted future recall were equal across conditions. One-week recall depended on whether retrieval practice continued, not on whether study continued.
numbers: Conditions ST and SNT (testing continued) recalled about 80% at 1 week; STN and SNTN (dropped from testing) recalled 36% and 33%. Repeated retrieval vs not: d = 4.03. Trials per condition: ST 320, SNT 236.8, STN 243.0, SNTN 154.8; about 80 extra study trials after first recall gave almost no gain. Predicted recall was about 50% in all four (20.3 to 22.0 of 40 items; F < 1). Students' predictions did not reflect the roughly 2.4x difference.
limits: Foreign-word pairs, free-recall tests, one lab. Authors say generalisation to other materials is inferred from the wider testing literature. Sample size was not extracted from the text read.
agent_relevance: Shows the cost of 'drop it once it is learned'. A scaffold that retires a skill the first time it passes will undertrain it, and the prediction data show learners cannot see this.

source: Cepeda, N. J., Pashler, H., Vul, E., Wixted, J. T., & Rohrer, D. (2006) Distributed practice in verbal recall tasks: A review and quantitative synthesis. Psychological Bulletin 132(3), 354-380
finding: Meta-analysis of the spacing effect. Spacing versus massing helped at every retention interval from under 1 minute to over 1 month. Beyond that contrast, lag between study episodes shows an inverted-U: the best inter-study interval grows with the retention interval. Evidence for expanding intervals was inconclusive.
numbers: 839 assessments in 317 experiments in 184 articles. Authors found no evidence that the spacing effect (equal total study time) is modulated by retention interval. Table 5 lag examples: 49.4% correct at 1-10 s lag vs 54.1% at 30-59 s (n.s., p = .167); 54.1% vs 48.8% for longer 1 min-3 h lags (n.s., p = .198), i.e. no reliable lag benefit at very short intervals. The feedback hypothesis for expanding intervals could not be tested adequately with current data.
limits: Verbal recall tasks only. Few studies had retention intervals beyond 1 day, so lag effects over long spans were thinly sampled (later addressed by Cepeda 2008). Heterogeneity is high.
agent_relevance: Foundation for any scheduling rule (spaced repetition, replay). Right level of confidence: spacing vs massing is solid; the best gap depends on how long the knowledge must last.

source: Cepeda, N. J., Vul, E., Rohrer, D., Wixted, J. T., & Pashler, H. (2008) Spacing effects in learning: A temporal ridgeline of optimal retention. Psychological Science 19(11), 1095-1102
finding: Large web study mapping gap by retention interval. More than 1,350 people learned facts, got a review after a gap of 0 to 105 days, and were tested up to 350 days after the review. Final recall first rose then fell as the gap grew; the best gap grew with the test delay but shrank as a share of it.
numbers: Optimal vs zero gap: 64% more recall, d = 1.1; 26% more recognition, d = 1.5. Optimal gaps tested, recall, at retention intervals 7, 35, 70, 350 days: 1, 11, 21, 21 days. Spline-interpolated: about 3, 8, 12, 27 days = 43%, 23%, 17%, 8% of the retention interval. Optimal gap fell from about 20-40% of a 1-week delay to 5-10% of a 1-year delay. Recall gain at the optimal gap: 10%, 59%, 111%, 77% for the four intervals. Fitted model: recall = A(1 + bt)^(-R), A = p + (1 - p)exp(-a g), R = 1 + c (ln(g + 1) - d)^2 with b = .011, p = .760, a = .017, c = .092, d = 3.453.
quote: the optimal gap declined from about 20 to 40% of a 1-week test delay to about 5 to 10% of a 1-year test delay
limits: Trivia facts, online sample, one study session plus one review. Authors call the fitted function 'a reasonable' one, not unique. Pavlik-Anderson style models could not fit both the rise of the best gap and the fall of its ratio to delay.
agent_relevance: A usable formal model of spacing. For an agent with a review or replay budget, set the gap from how long the memory must last, not as a fixed proportion.

source: Rowland, C. A. (2014) The effect of testing versus restudy on retention: A meta-analytic review of the testing effect. Psychological Bulletin 140(6), 1432-1463
finding: Meta-analysis of laboratory studies comparing testing to restudy. Reliable testing effect with high heterogeneity. Supports effortful-processing accounts: recall tests produced larger benefits than recognition tests. Describes the New Theory of Disuse and the bifurcation model as frameworks for why difficult retrieval helps.
numbers: Random-effects mean g = 0.50, 95% CI [0.42, 0.58], Z = 12.38; unweighted mean g = 0.54, median g = 0.55. Heterogeneity tau-squared = 0.21, Q = 1,009.42, I-squared = 84.35%. Describes Bjork & Bjork (1992): storage strength (how well learned) vs retrieval strength (how accessible now); difficult retrieval adds more storage strength.
limits: Laboratory studies only; classroom studies excluded. High heterogeneity means the average hides cases near zero or negative (the stem-and-leaf plot has effect sizes below 0). Feedback and initial test performance were coded as moderators.
agent_relevance: Typical size of a desirable-difficulty effect is medium (g about 0.5) and variable, so a single trial of one scaffold change is a weak test; plan for repeated measurement.

source: Donovan, J. J., & Radosevich, D. J. (1999) A meta-analytic review of the distribution of practice effect: Now you see it, now you don't. Journal of Applied Psychology 84(5), 795-805
finding: Meta-analysis showing the spaced-practice advantage depends on the task. It is big for simple physical tasks and near zero for complex tasks. Higher-rigor studies showed smaller effects.
numbers: 63 studies, 112 effect sizes. Overall d = 0.46 (95% CI 0.42 to 0.50), well below Lee & Genovese (1988) d = 0.96 (psychomotor only). Heterogeneity Q(111) = 1025.25. Task clusters: d = 0.97 (simple, low mental, high physical), 0.42 (high mental, average complexity), 0.11 and 0.07 (complex tasks). Task complexity correlated r = -.25 with effect size. Low-rigor studies gave larger effects.
limits: Mostly massed vs spaced within a session (intertrial rest), not days-long spacing. Does not directly address long-delay tests.
agent_relevance: Key boundary condition: the more complex the skill, the less spacing buys. Complex reasoning scaffolds may not gain from spacing operators; test before assuming.

source: Rohrer, D., & Taylor, K. (2007) The shuffling of mathematics problems improves learning. Instructional Science 35, 481-498
finding: Two college experiments on maths practice. Exp 1: practice on one problem type massed in one session or spaced over sessions, test a week later. Exp 2: four geometry-solid volume problem types, practice blocked by type or mixed, test a week later. Mixed practice made practice scores worse and test scores far better.
numbers: Exp 1 (66 students, permutations task): 1-week test accuracy 74% spaced vs 49% massers and 46% light massers; accuracy at the end of practice was equal (83% vs 82%). Exp 2: practice-session accuracy blockers 89% vs mixers 60% (t(16) = 3.14, d = 1.06); test blockers 20% vs mixers 63% (t(14) = 2.64, p < .05, d = 1.34). Students were taught all procedures first and could solve each type at the end of practice.
limits: Small samples in Exp 2 (about 16 students analysed). College students and well-defined formula problems; no transfer to real exams.
agent_relevance: Best human parallel to mixing task families for an agent: the mixed group has to choose the right procedure for each item, which is the skill needed at test time.

source: Kornell, N., Castel, A. D., Eich, T. S., & Bjork, R. A. (2010) Spacing as the friend of both memory and induction in young and older adults. Psychology and Aging 25(2), 498-503
finding: Replication and extension of Kornell & Bjork (2008) with older adults. Spacing helped both repetition learning (same painting repeated) and induction (different paintings per artist) in young and older adults. Participants of both ages rated massing as better for induction.
numbers: Spacing advantage F(1,108) = 27.32, partial eta-sq = .20; young beat older overall F(1,108) = 18.67. Older participants: 48 people, mean age 77. Induction ratings, young: 56% judged massing best, 19% spacing best, 25% same. Older: 75% massing, 4% spacing, 21% same. Repetition task, 59% of young and 38% of older judged spacing superior. 29% of young vs 6% of older said expertise helped; self-proclaimed experts did not do better (64% vs 60% correct).
limits: Same stimulus set and test type as the original. Older adults scored lower overall.
agent_relevance: Independent confirmation that the 'feels worse, works better' pattern holds for induction across ages, and that the illusion does not shrink with self-rated expertise.

source: Verkoeijen, P. P. J. L., & Bouwmeester, S. (2014) Is spacing really the 'friend of induction'? Frontiers in Psychology 5, 259
finding: Pre-planned high-powered exact replication of Kornell & Bjork (2008) Experiment 2 (the style-recognition test) with web (MTurk) participants. The spacing advantage replicated at similar size.
numbers: N = 123 (t(122)). First-block hit rate spaced 0.75 (SD .21) vs massed 0.66 (SD .22), t(122) = 4.18, p = 0.00005, d = 0.37; original reported 0.77 vs 0.67, d = 0.41. False alarms 0.48 vs 0.50, t(122) = 0.98, p = .33, d = 0.09. 71% (87 people) said massed presentation produced the most learning; 17% said both equal. Power 0.95 was planned for an expected d of about 0.33.
limits: Only the recognition experiment was replicated. Hit rates across later test blocks do not show a simple spaced advantage (block 2: massed 0.68 vs spaced 0.62) because test items act as extra learning; both studies use the first block.
agent_relevance: A clean successful replication with a different population; d of about 0.4 is a realistic prior for category-induction interleaving.

source: Donenfeld, J., Kaldy, Z., & Blaser, E. (2026) Testing the interleaving effect without response bias: A forced-choice reevaluation of Kornell & Bjork (2008). Psychonomic Bulletin & Review 33(6)
finding: Direct replication (N = 288, online) of K&B 2008 Exp 1A plus a conceptual replication that replaces artist identification by a 2-alternative forced-choice test, removing response-bias confounds. The interleaving effect held in both. Identification tests showed large differences in learning and response bias across categories, but biases were similar between conditions.
numbers: Exp 1 (identification; 358 recruited, 288 analysed): blocked M = 0.29, interleaved M = 0.38, t(287) = 8.08, dz = 0.48, CI [0.36, 0.59]. Exp 2 (2AFC; 365 recruited, 276 analysed): t(275) = 7.19, dz = 0.43, CI [0.32, 0.55]. Some artists were learned up to 3.3x better than others; participants used their most-used response 5x more often than their least-used one. In the Exp 2 results text the means read interleaved 0.73 and blocked 0.79, which contradicts the positive effect (probably swapped labels).
limits: Prolific participants aged 18-30; TOST equivalence bound dz = 0.2. Authors state nearly all direct replications used identification, a design confounding memory and response bias, including the 59 studies in Brunmair & Richter (2019).
agent_relevance: Evidence that the interleaving effect is not a test artefact. Design lesson for us: measure with forced choice or calibrated scoring, not a single hit rate.

source: Kornell, N., Hays, M. J., & Bjork, R. A. (2009) Unsuccessful retrieval attempts enhance subsequent learning. JEP: Learning, Memory, and Cognition 35(4), 989-998
finding: A failed attempt to answer a question, followed by the answer, beats the same time spent reading the answer. Tested with fictional trivia questions (Exp 1-2) and with cue words whose target is a weak associate (Exp 3-6), where correct guesses were removed from analyses.
numbers: Exp 1 (25 students): final cued recall .41 test vs .31 read-only, t(24) = 2.97, d = 0.58. Later experiments with weak associates gave advantages with d between 0.38 and 1.49 (examples: .71 vs .50, d = 1.49, n = 15; .67 vs .55, d = 0.38; .47 vs .35, d = 0.94). Errors of omission vs commission did not differ in later recall (e.g. .64 blank vs .70 wrong, n.s.).
limits: Small samples per experiment. The answer was shown after each attempt (feedback present). High error rates without feedback were not tested.
agent_relevance: Supports letting the agent attempt first and see the reference answer after; wrong attempts are not wasted.

source: Kornell, N., & Son, L. K. (2009) Learners' choices and beliefs about self-testing. Memory 17(5), 493-501
finding: Mismatch between beliefs and choices. Participants judged restudy ('pair mode') as better than cued testing, while testing in fact gave higher recall; yet when given the choice they tested themselves, mostly to diagnose what they knew rather than to learn.
numbers: Exp 1 (35 participants, F(1,33)): final accuracy higher in test mode, F = 7.60, partial eta-sq = .19; judgments of learning higher for pair mode, F = 7.74. Exp 2 (choice): by list 4, with feedback, testing was chosen above 50%, t(15) = 4.39, d = 1.10; without feedback not significant (t(18) = 1.16). Pilot: choosers who tested on 55% of trials matched all-test recall (63%) and beat all-pair (37%). Survey: most reported testing to diagnose memory.
limits: Word-pair flashcards, small samples. Choice of testing reached significance only when tests were followed by feedback.
agent_relevance: Agents, like people, may like checking themselves but undervalue testing as a learning event. A scaffold can use checks as training, not only as grading.

source: Bjork, R. A., Dunlosky, J., & Kornell, N. (2013) Self-regulated learning: Beliefs, techniques, and illusions. Annual Review of Psychology 64, 417-444
finding: Review of how learners misjudge their own learning. Learners treat fluency (retrieval, encoding, perceptual) as a sign of learning, so easy conditions are preferred even when they harm long-term learning. Desirable difficulties (spacing, interleaving, generating, self-testing, varying conditions) impair performance during acquisition but help long-term learning.
numbers: Reports Kornell (2009): 90% of college participants did better after spaced than massed practice, yet 72% said massing was more effective after the session. Reports a generation experiment: 8 s generating a wrong answer plus 5 s study beats 13 s study. Shows the Kornell & Bjork (2008) judged-vs-actual figure for 120 participants.
limits: A review; numbers are second-hand. The Kornell (2009) 90% and 72% figures were read only through this review.
agent_relevance: The clearest short statement of the bias our agent inherits: it will tend to prefer whichever scaffold makes its own traces look fluent.

source: Landauer, T. K., & Bjork, R. A. (1978) Optimum rehearsal patterns and name learning (in Gruneberg, Morris & Sykes, Practical Aspects of Memory)
finding: Expanding retrieval practice. For test-type practice (a fact shown once, then self-tested), rehearsals at increasing intervals gave the best name recall; for restudy-type practice (the item is re-presented) uniform spacing was slightly better.
numbers: Fixed number of rehearsals in a fixed period; abstract states increasing intervals best for test-type practice, uniform spacing slightly better when information was repeated. Exact percentages were not extracted from the scan.
quote: a pattern of increasing intervals between successive rehearsals was best for test-type practice
limits: Later work (Cepeda 2006) found expanding vs equal intervals mixed, possibly dependent on feedback. Short chapter; cell sizes not extracted.
agent_relevance: The earliest formal link between retrieval difficulty and scheduling: retest only after some forgetting, the same logic as review-scheduling replay for models.

source: Sana, F., & Yan, V. X. (2022) Interleaving retrieval practice promotes science learning. Psychological Science 33(5), 782-788
finding: Classroom test of two difficulties combined. In 4 weeks of weekly science quizzes, concepts quizzed in interleaved order were remembered better a month later than concepts quizzed in blocked order, which beat concepts not quizzed.
numbers: N = 155 grade 9-12 students. Month-later test: not quizzed M = 47% (SD 20), blocked quiz M = 54% (SD 28), interleaved quiz M = 63% (SD 26). Blocked vs not quizzed d = 0.30; interleaved vs blocked d = 0.35; interleaved vs not quizzed d = 0.71. A secondary analysis gave interleaved 58% vs blocked 51% (d = 0.27). An earlier study cited in the introduction reported d = 0.83 for interleaving.
limits: Two teachers' science classes, with section-level random assignment; effects are moderate. Classroom control is weaker than lab control.
agent_relevance: Evidence that the lab result survives in a real classroom and stacks: retrieval plus interleaving beat either alone. Design hint: interleave the self-tests.

source: Settles, B., & Meeder, B. (2016) A trainable spaced repetition model for language learning (half-life regression). ACL 2016
finding: Computational model of spacing. Half-life regression predicts the memory half-life of each word for each learner from history and features, with recall probability p = 2^(-lag/half-life). Fit on Duolingo logs, it cut error by 45%+ versus simple schedulers and improved engagement in A/B tests.
numbers: 12.9 million instances (90/10 train/test). Mean absolute error of recall probability: HLR 0.128, Leitner 0.235, Pimsleur 0.445, logistic regression 0.211, constant guess 0.175. AUC values were 0.51 to 0.54 for all. A/B test 1 (HLR vs Leitner): just under 1 million students, 6 weeks, slight rise in overall activity and new lessons but a significant drop in practice sessions. A/B test 2: HLR without lexeme tags vs HLR, 3.3 million students, 2 weeks, all three retention metrics rose significantly.
limits: Predicts recall of vocabulary in an app, not learning transfer. AUC near 0.5 means weak ranking. Retention A/B outcomes measure engagement (return next day), not learning gains.
agent_relevance: A deployed spacing model. A half-life-per-item model is a ready design for scheduling an agent's skill reviews, but validate against actual long-delay accuracy, not engagement.

source: Ge, Y., Li, X., Li, W., & Li, X. (2021) What is the mechanism underlying the interleaving effect in category induction: An eye-tracking study. Frontiers in Psychology 12, 770885
finding: Tests two accounts of why interleaving helps category learning: attention attenuation (blocked learners attend less to later same-category items) versus discriminative contrast (interleaving puts different categories side by side). Eye-tracking did not support attention attenuation as the main mechanism; raising discriminative contrast improved learning.
numbers: Exp 1 and 2: 12 artists, fixed-pace and self-paced learning, fixation duration by position in block. Exp 3: high-contrast condition performed significantly better than medium- and low-contrast conditions (main effect of contrast significant). Sample sizes not extracted.
limits: Chinese college samples; painting stimuli. Does not rule out other accounts such as sequential comparison or retrieval.
agent_relevance: Mechanism hint: interleaving works by placing contrasting categories in comparison. For an agent, interleave near-confusable problem types rather than random ones.

source: Javadi group (corresponding author A.-H. Javadi) (2025) Does difficulty moderate learning? A comparative analysis of the desirable difficulties framework and cognitive load theory. Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology 78(10), 2181-2195
finding: Competing-theory review. Desirable difficulties (and the retrieval effort hypothesis) say more effort improves retention; cognitive load theory says extraneous load hurts. Proposes a combined model: raise difficulty for low-element-interactivity material (focus, retention), lower it for high-element-interactivity material to avoid overload.
numbers: No new data; a theoretical integration with perceptual load theory. Model rule: tune difficulty to material complexity and learner expertise.
limits: Narrative review, the proposed model is untested. It echoes the expertise-reversal pattern (subfield 02) and Donovan & Radosevich on task complexity.
agent_relevance: Decision rule for when to add difficulty: not for heavy many-interacting-parts tasks or novices; yes for simple or already-mastered material.

source: Song, Y., Kim, H., & Kim, T. (2026) A minimal recurrent neural network models the robustness of interleaved practice on motor sequence learning. Scientific Reports 16
finding: An Elman recurrent network trained on three seven-step finger-tap sequences under blocked (repetitive) or interleaved practice reproduces the human pattern: faster training-loss decline under blocked practice, but better trained-set performance, better generalisation to new sequences and less interference under interleaving.
numbers: Pretrained on 10 arbitrary sequences; then 15,000 trials on 3 new sequences, batch 20. Tests: trained set, 100 novel sequences, weight noise, weight pruning, interference from a new sequence. Quantitative tables not extracted.
limits: Tiny network and a motor-sequence task, explains the benefit by input variability plus recurrence only. Not an LLM.
agent_relevance: A minimal neural model where the practice-versus-test reversal appears without special memory machinery, so the reversal can appear in artificial learners.

source: Russin, J., Pavlick, E., & Frank, M. J. (2024; PNAS 2025) The dynamic interplay between in-context and in-weight learning in humans and neural networks
finding: A metalearning transformer with in-context learning (ICL) and in-weight learning (IWL) reproduces a human curriculum split. For rule-like tasks, blocked order is better (ICL infers the rule). When tasks lack easy rules, interleaving is better, because blocking causes catastrophic forgetting in weights.
numbers: Human compositional task: 47 of 58 participants generalised after blocked trials vs 36 of 60 after interleaved. In networks: interleaved better than blocked in the rotated non-rule task (p < 10^-3) due to forgetting when blocked; rule-like task with blocked trials reached near-perfect few-shot accuracy. Task-by-curriculum interaction in category learning p = 0.04.
limits: Metalearning transformers on synthetic tasks as an account of LLM-style ICL; not a test of large pretrained LLMs on school tasks.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition for desirable difficulties in AI: when structure is rule-like and can be inferred in context, blocked presentation can win; interleaving protects weight-based learning from forgetting.

source: Atreya, A., Batra, D., Mantri, Y. K., Bantug, G., Cowan, G. A., & Khraishi, R. (2026) When to review: Spaced repetition for continual pre-training of language models (SRT)
finding: Uses the SuperMemo-2 scheduler inside LLM continual pre-training. Each replayed example has an ease factor, review count, interval and due step; per-example perplexity becomes a recall-quality score. Against uniform replay and a difficulty-only baseline on temporally separated Wikipedia and code corpora, spaced scheduling kept more old knowledge while still learning new.
numbers: Source-grounded QA, 500 old + 500 new questions per domain. TinyLlama-1.1B Wikipedia: base old 54.3%; naive CPT old 11.7%, new 17.0% (base new 13.1%); uniform replay old 25.2%; PPL-prioritised old 27.4%, new 38.8%; SRT old 49.0%, new 20.0%. Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct Wikipedia: base old 50.2%; CPT old 43.0%; uniform replay 46.2%; SRT old 51.6%, new 42.4%. SRT recovers 5 to 37 points of old accuracy lost by naive CPT. Gap SRT vs uniform replay: 23.8 points on TinyLlama, 5.4 on Llama-3B. Llama-3B GSM8K falls from 77.6% to 38.8% under CPT and 6.8% under uniform replay, while SRT keeps 57.8/52.6/76.7/74.3 on MMLU, BBH, GSM8K, PIQA. Overhead vs uniform replay about +14.7%.
limits: Scheduling is by perplexity, with no delayed-test counterfactual that isolates a 'desirable difficulty' effect. SRT trades plasticity for retention (TinyLlama new 20.0% vs 38.8% for the difficulty-only baseline). Small models, two corpora, bootstrap SDs of about 2 points.
agent_relevance: The closest LLM test of spacing as a scheduler: interval-based review beat random replay at equal exposure. The difficulty-only baseline learned new facts faster but kept less old knowledge, the performance-versus-retention split in miniature.

source: Prakriya, N., Yen, J.-N., Hsieh, C.-J., & Cong, J. (2024/2025) Accelerating large language model pretraining via LFR pedagogy: Learn, Focus, and Review
finding: Pretraining that tracks per-block perplexity, up-weights blocks the model tends to forget, and reviews them, inspired by spaced repetition. Claims lower perplexity and higher downstream accuracy with a fraction of the tokens.
numbers: Llama models on SlimPajama and GPT models on OpenWebText. Uses only 5% to 19% of the training tokens of full-data baselines; matched Pythia models with up to 2x the parameters using 3.2% of their tokens; in one analysis 78.5% of sampled blocks showed forgetting-like loss behaviour; higher accuracy than Pythia in 55.55% of task-model cases (e.g. a 120M LFR model on 50B tokens vs Pythia-160M on 300B).
limits: Author-run baselines; the Pythia comparison involves different data. Does not separate spacing from plain hard-example selection (a curriculum effect). Task-level tables only partly read.
agent_relevance: A proof of concept that reviewing items near forgetting helps LLM training, but confounded with hard-example focus.

source: Brunmair, M., & Richter, T. (2019) Similarity matters: A meta-analysis of interleaved learning and its moderators. Psychological Bulletin 145(11), 1029-1052 (second-hand via Donenfeld et al. 2026)
finding: Cited by Donenfeld et al. as a main meta-analysis of interleaving; they say its 59 inductive category-learning studies share the identification test design. Primary text not opened.
numbers: Not read here. Donenfeld et al. give only the count of 59 studies. A pooled effect figure from memory (about g = 0.4, larger for paintings than for words or maths) is unverified.
limits: Second-hand; any numbers beyond the study count are unverified.
agent_relevance: Open item for angle B: read the primary paper for moderators, especially stimulus similarity.

source: Bjork, R. A., & Bjork, E. L. (1992) A new theory of disuse and an old theory of stimulus fluctuation (in Healy, Kosslyn & Shiffrin, From Learning Processes to Cognitive Processes) (second-hand via Rowland 2014)
finding: Theory behind desirable difficulties. Each memory has a storage strength (how well learned) and a retrieval strength (how accessible now). Per Rowland's description, difficult tests add more to memory when retrieval strength is lower, so conditions that lower retrieval strength during practice can raise storage strength more. Performance during learning tracks retrieval strength; durable learning is storage strength.
numbers: Described via Rowland (2014), who cites p. 42 for storage strength 'well learned'. The primary chapter was not opened; no equations read.
limits: Second-hand description. Verbal in what was read; no fitted parameters seen.
agent_relevance: Gives the formal story for why immediate gain misleads: it measures retrieval strength. Design principle: measure after retrieval strength has decayed.

source: Yan, V. X., Bjork, E. L., & Bjork, R. A. (2016) On the difficulty of mending metacognitive illusions: A priori theories, fluency effects, and misattributions of the interleaving benefit. JEP: General 145(7), 918-933 (second-hand via Donenfeld et al. 2026)
finding: Cited by Donenfeld et al. as showing that learners' appraisals of learning are higher for blocked than interleaved conditions. Primary text not opened.
numbers: Not read here.
limits: Second-hand citation only.
agent_relevance: Open item: read Yan et al. to see which interventions reduced the illusion; relevant to making an agent distrust its own confidence in blocked lessons.
